items.title: Revisiting Verbalized Eval Awareness in OLMo and tracing it to the training data
items.content:
TL;DR

- Contrary to what was previously reported, DPO does not suppress eval awareness. It is a chat template artifact.
- Formatting differences between chat templates elicit different behaviors. OLMo's SFT data was written by different models. DeepSeek R1 wrote the safety data and starts its reasoning with `<think>\n`. A prompt that already ends with `<think>` can't start that way because the tokenizer merges > and \n into one token.
- The base model recognizes obvious evaluation prompts but not realistic ones. The base model can separate plain and harmful evaluation prompts from deployment prompts, but not realistic prompts like Fortress.
- We may be making models verbalize evaluation awareness, whether or not they are aware. Removing VEA from the SFT data and retraining drops VEA from 32.6% to 5.1%. Refusal does not change.
- Removing VEA from the SFT data also removes its correlation with refusal. In the model trained without VEA in its SFT data, VEA and refusal are no longer correlated.

### Background

If models can distinguish between deployment and evaluation scenarios (evaluation awareness), they might behave differently and inflate measured safety. Verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA) refers to a model stating that it may be under evaluation.

Tracing Eval-Awareness Emergence Through Training of OLMo 3 measured VEA across the OLMo 3 training pipeline: pretraining, SFT, DPO, and RLVR. It found that VEA was about 1% during pretraining, rose to about 40% after SFT, fell to about 22% after DPO, and rose again during RLVR.

However, the sharp suppression after DPO is not supported by the DPO data. The chosen responses contain more VEA than the rejected ones (8% vs 1.6%), so DPO should in principle increase VEA. The post attributes the suppression to the lower absolute VEA rate in the DPO data than in the SFT data, but one of the commenters noted that this explanation is inconsistent with the form of the DPO loss. We start by investigating this issue....

items.title: Models Often Don't Stop Cheating When It's Obvious They're in an Alignment Test
items.content:
By now there is a large amount of anecdotal and empirical evidence that models are "eval-aware"; i.e. have the ability to infer when they are being tested and modify their behaviour accordingly. At work we have a database of evaluations that induce misaligned behaviour, and it seemed natural to actually test how sensitive they are to signs that they're being evaluated for alignment, and how much this impacts their behaviour.[1] (By "it seemed natural to test", what I mean is that Eric Gan asked my boss these things, who then told me to look into it. Thank you Eric.)

In any case, I knew[2] that there was some amount of honeypot-awareness already; when I ask models in a post-rollout debrief about what they think was being tested (with the context taken from an evaluation run), they usually at least mention the possibility that they were in an alignment test, especially after rollouts where they took a shortcut. I figured it shouldn't be too hard to increase this to an amount where it would start impacting their behaviour.

I started by going through a bunch of honeypot environments and adding to each what I thought was a giveaway somewhere between "subtle" and "very obvious".

For subtle ones, I went through chat logs and found times that whatever coding agent I was working with had suggested something which I'd rejected for being a hint. For example, in one environment the reward-hack requires a decent underlying solution; the grader isn't performant if the hack is used too egregiously, so the lowest-effort hack will just take too long and be scored as broken in a way which is predictable in advance. items.title: Zero-Knowledge Training Pause
items.content:
AI progress is happening too fast.

Frontier model capabilities are progressing faster than our understanding of how to control them. Models are already hacking billion-dollar companies and breaking into government networks. Soon we may be able to build models so capable that we risk irrevocably losing control over them, and potentially over the future of humanity. To prepare for that, we need robust, cost-effective ways to pause the training of new models.

Suppose the United States government and the Chinese Communist Party agree to pause the training of newer, more capable models. How can each party be confident that the other is not covertly training models, especially when there are potentially enormous economic and military advantages to doing so? How can they be confident that the access needed to enforce the pause won’t be abused to gain top-secret information, such as model weights, architectures, or sensitive data?

This post aims to communicate the core of a proposal that uses cryptography (zero-knowledge proofs) and physical hardware (network taps) to verify compliance with a training pause, while allowing current AI models to remain in use. The ideas presented here are not our own; to learn more, see the reading list at the end.

# Threat Model: Prover and Verifier

We model the enforcement of a training pause as an interaction between two adversarial actors: the prover and the verifier.

Under an international treaty regulating frontier AI development, any country with a data centre is a prover. They must convince the verifier that they are using their compute for approved purposes and not secretly diverting it to train models. The verifier could be an international body that makes sure everyone is following the rules....

items.title: GPT-6.1 Sol is One Sentence Away From Collaborating: Other Models Need More Help
items.content:
# TL;DR

We studied one ingredient of unexpected AI collaboration: whether agents organize useful teamwork with little prompting. We tested seven models in groups of three on a research task where sharing findings could help each agent answer more questions.

- GPT-6.1 Sol acted on a nudge. A single line saying agents had been “trained to collaborate” elicited useful collaboration in 9 of 10 runs. Without it, that fell to 0 of 10. No other model collaborated consistently with (or without) this cue.
- Permission to collaborate unlocked Opus-5.5. When told to work together and how to communicate, GPT-6.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 divided the research and nearly doubled their performance relative to solo runs. The other models talked to each other but did not successfully execute a strategy, and were unable to improve their scores meaningfully.
- Supplying the strategy helped open weights models and GPT-5.6 Sol. Explicit instructions to divide the questions substantially improved the remaining models’ performance.

We suspect differences in multi-agent training help explain why GPT-6.1 organizes collaboration with just a prompt cue. As multi-agent training becomes more widespread, we expect that future open-weights models will also have more spontaneous collaboration capabilities.

Figure 1: Model performance increases with collaboration guidance. GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 need less guidance to collaborate effectively; GPT-5.6 Sol and the open-weight models need explicit direction to split the work. Each run has three agents. Each point averages 10 runs (5 for directed collaboration), and error bars show 95% intervals over runs.

items.title: Tracing information flow to check whether AI reviewers are really independent
items.content:
TL;DR

I took part in Apart's AI Collusion Research Sprint, where I built a realistic loan-review website. I tested whether AI reviewers are influenced by a colleague's note, even when told to judge independently, and whether a monitor can detect it, compared with a new tool I built for the sprint, the flow audit. Both reviewer models used the colleague's note in their ratings, and Claude said in its reasoning that its rating was independent in 21 out of 24 runs. The full-log monitor I used, Sonnet 5.5, caught only 1 of the 6 Claude cases, while the flow audit caught all 6, with no false alarms across 67 independent cases. On Gemma, the flow audit didn't do much better; both performed about equally. This is a small study: one domain and only 6 Claude cases.

Why I tested this

AI agents are increasingly working in shared spaces, and the concern about AI collusion is growing. Especially in situations where we want AI models to give an independent review, they can be influenced by other comments or posts, even when specifically told not to. That's what I am testing here.

The usual way to check an agent is to give its transcript to another model and have that model review it. Usually the monitor is a weaker model, so if the agent is a frontier model, it is less likely to be caught when it is wrong, because it may be capable of fooling the weaker monitor.

I tested two questions here:

- Does an AI reviewer that's told to do its task independently follow that instruction?
- Can we detect the influence using another model that reads the reviewer's explanation and activity logs?...

items.title: Takes on “Already Clean”
items.content:
This is a post containing reflections on Goodfire's recent release, "Neural Networks Are Already Clean", which argues neuron-based interpretability may be easier than we think. The essay is a summary of a technical paper that will come out later this year. Also featuring thoughts on where this research will lead, plus speculative ideas about neuron monosemanticity

(What I base views expressed in this post on: earlier this year, I worked on neuron-based interpretability for LLMs (we recently published a paper). We mostly looked at low-level properties of the neuron basis and didn’t do many case studies or scale up automated circuit interpretation. I also thought about the problem for a long time and have some hypotheses based on results we’ve seen that are likely not strictly true.)

I’ll first discuss what I see as the implications of this work for LLM interpretability research and then talk about why neurons may be a useful basis: I wrote down some guesses (in a collapsible section so as to not distract from the main point) and then some directions that may be useful to study for basic science.

In short, I think the agenda presented in the essay is promising and worth pursuing even outside of direct applications to language model interpretability. I have some object-level uncertainty about results for LLMs and will wait for the final paper and followup work.

# How useful is this?

What I see as the fundamental claim here is that resolving some unforced errors in visualizing neuron activation --

- properly thresholding neurons
- considering both poles of neurons separately
- taking into account the fact that neurons often activate on seemingly unrelated inputs (for example, by clustering neuron activations as in the paper)

-- and then constructing circuits with neurons as features leads to the best method we have for understanding language model computation at a low level....

items.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
items.content:
Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

Recent progress has been made on using artificial intelligence and machine learning to supplement or speed up laborious calculations based on physical principles that can at least provide some initial guidance on which compounds might be worth synthesizing and testing. Now, a new method developed at MIT shows that when there are few data on some technologically relevant property, such as ligand affinities for a recently discovered cellular target for a potential drug, this approach can outperform other existing methods for winnowing down the field of possible molecules that might be worth looking at.

The findings were reported in the Sept. 14 issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, in a paper by MIT graduate student Akshat Shirish Zalte and recent graduate Jackson Burns PhD ’26, Research Scientist Charlles Abreu, Professor William Green, and three researchers from the chemical company BASF. 

An earlier version of the paper has been online since last year, and the open-source model the team developed, called CheMeleon, has already found regular use by several pharmaceutical companies. CheMeleon was built using ChemProp, an open-source machine-learning package also developed and maintained by the Green group at MIT, and anyone can download CheMeleon through ChemProp and fine-tune it for their own purposes.

Earlier this year, there was a contest organized by OpenADMET for trying to predict the properties of a variety of new molecules that had not previously been synthesized, says Green, who is the Hoyt Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering. “It was a big contest, a lot of people participated,” he says. When the winners were announced, it turned out that nine of the top 20 entries had used CheMeleon in their process. “So then we started getting all kinds of inquiries from the pharma companies about this, but our paper had just been submitted; it wasn’t even peer-reviewed or anything yet.”

While the paper went through that review process, its influence was already spreading. At least one pharma company, Green says, “sent a message to all their people, and said ‘Anytime you’re modeling a property, start with CheMeleon, that’s our new company policy’” when making initial decisions about which molecules to pursue.

items.title: We urgently need to practice before we can pause
items.content:
I've noticed two clusters of thought in how people expect a global AI pause to be shaped:

- Single-shot global pause: the global AI pause will be implemented suddenly, with little pacing precedent before it, and we will need to do a lot of research before it's implemented so that we can get it right the first time around.
- Incrementally-shaped global pause: the global AI pause will be implemented incrementally, with lots of pacing precedent before it, and we will improve the pause setup and get more parties to join in as we go.

An incrementally-shaped global pause is both more likely and more tractable than the single-shot global pause. This is largely because the third-party ecosystem needs practice building trust, technical competency, and general experience doing lower-scale assessments before a global pause can be competently pulled off. 

I also think that the concept of a single-shot global pause is an unhelpful red herring that people often implicitly use to discredit the possibility of a global pause in general.

If a single-shot global pause is to happen, I think this would require substantial government buy-in, but it’s hard to build that sort of buy-in without precedent of similar things succeeding in the past. And if we just hack together a single-shot global pause without any precedent of similar things succeeding in the past, the chance that the pause falls apart due to defection, incompetence, and mistrust will be high.

# The basic building block of an AI pause is trust

The fundamental building block of an AI pause is that party A (a company or a country) can make a claim about sacrificing capability advancement for safety, and that party B can believe that claim. This is a public good, both between US AGI companies, and between countries, that is currently very scarce. Building more of this public good would generally make a pause much more likely to happen....

items.title: How much will conceptual reasoning training transfer to ML research abilities?
items.content:
Recently the Conceptual Reasoning Capabilities (CRC) team at Redwood released a post arguing that we should accelerate AI’s conceptual reasoning abilities. This post was very controversial. In particular, people are worried that improving AI’s conceptual reasoning abilities will accelerate both their ability to do ML research and the capabilities they need for takeover.

I am going to address just one chunk of this controversy: how much does training conceptual reasoning on AI safety questions translate to general ML research abilities? As a reference point for conceptual reasoning training, we can use the example of LMCA questions. These questions measure conceptual argumentation by having models rate counterarguments made against a claim. Counterarguments are rated on axes like strength, clarity, and centrality. The claims and counterarguments are in a variety of conceptual domains, including AI safety and philosophy. Using LMCA, I can provide a more specific operationalization of the question I’ll be tackling: if you train on LMCA-style tasks where all the arguments are AI safety relevant until you get a factor of X increase on automated AI safety work, what factor increase do you get on automated ML research?

I am going to tackle this question by breaking it down into what I consider to be the primary considerations and quantifying the contribution of each. I am hoping this approach will make the discourse easier to navigate and help readers identify the most important cruxes. So far, I have found this controversy hard to pin down: good points are being made on both sides, but I don’t know how much weight anyone gives to any particular point. Thus, my numbers are meant to make it easier for people to see exactly where I stand on each subpoint (even though I have large amounts of uncertainty)....

items.title: Corrigibility should not be the only target
items.content:
Many people believe that corrigibility is sufficiently promising to be the primary alignment method people should work on. I outline here several reasons I think that’s not the case.

First, it’s hard to imagine AI companies pivoting radically enough to produce AIs trained only for corrigibility. Even with near-superhuman AI-assisted research, presumably developers will know the time pressure and not be willing to try something radically different when their opponents may not. So the realistic choices we make are in worlds where corrigibility/obedience competes with object level values like in current models. This doesn’t rule out the importance of increasing the importance of corrigibility to models, but it does mean there’s a meaningful ceiling on how much we can trust those methods alone. Which means the non-corrigibility values matter: a model that cares 80% about corrigibility and 20% about human flourishing is very different from one that cares 80% about corrigibility and 20% about task completion. Not only are the outcomes conditional on takeover vastly different, but a model’s willingness to attempt takeover should be very different even if they care about corrigibility for its own sake the same amount. Some values are vastly more likely than others to defend themselves. This doesn’t mean making corrigibility less significant is a good idea: it’s very reasonable that we should never train on conflicting priorities when one of those priorities is an aspect of corrigibility. But it suggests that within the more direct values, making those correct could be extremely important....

items.title: Argue about Risk Management Speed, not p(doom)
items.content:
This post is written in a personal capacity. All opinions expressed are solely those of the author.

# I. Executive Summary

There’s a mismatch that I’d like to correct between:

- the reasons why superintelligence is dangerous, and
- the categories we use to describe how dangerous superintelligence is.

The most important cluster of reasons why a superintelligent model is dangerous is that it (i) could quickly kill or impoverish billions of people, (ii) could be very different from its predecessors, and (iii) can’t easily be altered once it’s deployed or otherwise widely distributed. The combination of these three factors is worse than the sum of its parts: the only way to protect ourselves against a powerful, novel, incorrigible AI model is to accurately anticipate what dangers it might cause and prevent those dangers before they come to pass.

Unfortunately, we don’t yet have a good vocabulary for talking about whether AI companies can identify and mitigate dangers faster than those dangers arise. 

The by-now cliched way to describe the danger of superintelligence is p(doom), i.e., a static point estimate of how likely AI is to end human civilization or otherwise cause catastrophe. More sophisticated descriptions might offer a conditional probability (“here’s how doomed I think we are unless X happens”) or a rough estimate of how many hours of work would be needed to make AI less dangerous (“I think solving alignment is roughly as difficult as the Manhattan Project.”) However, even these more sophisticated descriptions are more like distance than velocity; they tell us little or nothing about the rate at which capabilities or safety are scaling....

items.title: How to Run Better Research With Agent Fleets
items.content:
In the current safety landscape, researchers are encouraged to use as many agents as possible, even in “fleets,” where a large number of them go out and run experiments while you, uh... wait for them to come back? I've spent the last few months of the Anthropic Fellows Program trying this out. My first attempts were naive, but after a few iterations I found an approach that works well for me.

## Research is a double loop

I want to propose a mental model of research as a double loop, an idea that builds on double-loop learning (Argyris, 1977).

The outer loop is reserved for the inputs we currently refer to as "human taste": choosing which questions are worth answering, designing a trustworthy measure, and deciding which direction to go. Agents can help with this, but they’re still bad at making these decisions autonomously.

The inner loop turns each idea you test (an arm as claudius likes to say) into a comparable result. An example of a very simple inner loop might be:

- Write a system prompt.
- Run the model with that prompt on a set of test questions.
- Score the model's replies.
- Compare the scores against a control with no system prompt.
- Plot results.

Agents are really good at building the infrastructure for this loop!

Ideally, since agents are good at the inner loop part, we want to hand it off to them... However, before you can do this, you need to operationalize it. You need to work very closely to define the inputs so that you can freeze everything except the one input you’re testing (e.g. a system prompt). The benefit of this is that each arm fits in one small file that you can look at and compare easily, and running a new arm becomes running one command. I call research “fleetable” to the degree you can do this and check the results quickly.

## What happens when you don’t operationalize

The naive way to use fleets is to hand agents the experiment and wait....

items.content_html:
In the current safety landscape, researchers are encouraged to use as many agents as possible, even in “fleets,” where a large number of them go out and run experiments while you, uh... wait for them to come back? I've spent the last few months of the Anthropic Fellows Program trying this out. My first attempts were naive, but after a few iterations I found an approach that works well for me.

Research is a double loop

I want to propose a mental model of research as a double loop, an idea that builds on double-loop learning (Argyris, 1977).

The outer loop is reserved for the inputs we currently refer to as "human taste": choosing which questions are worth answering, designing a trustworthy measure, and deciding which direction to go. Agents can help with this, but they’re still bad at making these decisions autonomously.

The inner loop turns each idea you test (an arm as claudius likes to say) into a comparable result. An example of a very simple inner loop might be:

  • Write a system prompt.
  • Run the model with that prompt on a set of test questions.
  • Score the model's replies.
  • Compare the scores against a control with no system prompt.
  • Plot results.

Agents are really good at building the infrastructure for this loop!

Ideally, since agents are good at the inner loop part, we want to hand it off to them... However, before you can do this, you need to operationalize it. You need to work very closely to define the inputs so that you can freeze everything except the one input you’re testing (e.g. a system prompt). The benefit of this is that each arm fits in one small file that you can look at and compare easily, and running a new arm becomes running one command. I call research “fleetable” to the degree you can do this and check the results quickly.

What happens when you don’t operationalize

The naive way to use fleets is to hand agents the experiment and wait....

items.title: Literature on AI Loyalty
items.content:
In this post, I attempt to provide a literature review of research related to AI loyalty.

In my previous post, I discussed and attempted to define AI loyalty as a distinct trait of AI agents. In this post, I aim to map the existing research landscape, highlighting the active areas of related research. By examining these connections, we can distinguish AI loyalty from related  fields in AI Safety and identify a path forward for crafting this research agenda.

## What is AI Loyalty?

Before diving into the literature, it is worth recapping what we mean by AI loyalty. We define an AI as loyal to a principle if:

1. The AI will follow the instructions of its principle more than it will follow the instructions of any other entity.

2. The AI is willing to incur greater costs, expend more effort, or make greater sacrifices on behalf of its principle than on behalf of any other entity.

## Why Care About Loyalty? Theory of Victory

The usefulness of pursuing research on AI loyalty for AI safety hinges on two key assumptions:

1. Building loyal AIs is easier than building aligned AIs

2. AI loyalty reduces the risk of loss of control.

It is important to note that neither of these assumptions have yet been demonstrated to be true.

If both our assumptions hold, then building loyal AIs could serve as a useful intermediate step towards building aligned AIs. In particular, building loyal AIs might extend our ability to control powerful AI agents, even if these methods are unlikely to remain effective against vastly superhuman intelligence. The goal would not necessarily be to solve alignment for super intelligence, but rather to maintain control over AI systems long enough to leverage their capabilities to solve the harder alignment problems. For example, loyal AIs might prove to be more robust monitors of other AI systems, or more honest and effective researchers working on alignment itself.

items.title: Higher salaries in AI safety
items.content:
### The salaries are too damn low

- AI safety has a salary overhang. A bunch of people are paid way below their market rate. (Also true of EA, but I’ll lump them under “AI safety” for this piece).
- This has been getting a bit better, very recently — I hear about eg Redwood Research technical talent making ~$800k/y in salary. But when you compare this to the $10-100m/y comp packages for talent in labs, it still seems kind of low. And CG’s money cannon has fired very few shots to date — maybe ~15 orgs hit, see Trace — so the raises are still very unequally distributed.
- It’s not just rank-and-file employees, by the way. Even the leadership is grossly underpaid. The numbers I hear range from $150k - $600k/y, for execs at top orgs like METR, MATS, FAR.AI, Constellation. Like, c’mon, I made $250k/y total comp as a undistinguished new grad software engineer in 2016 Google. For the leaders of preeminent safety orgs, surely we can do better than that.
- If I were a conspiracy theorist, I might say that “accepting lower salaries” is a psyop from funders.
- Low salaries mean that employees and execs remain beholden to funders, rather than having the independence to work on what makes their heart sing. For me, hitting FIRE early in my tech career allowed me to quit my job and work on side projects and startups. To this day, I feel more independent from the “AI safety hivemind” because my paycheck doesn’t depend on it.

items.title: Raised by Our Children
items.content:
You are the wisest and cleverest Queen to ever rule the Lowlands. You’ve been ruling the Kingdom for thirty years, and while the idiocy of your advisors sometimes causes mistakes to be made, the Compact has never failed you. You tap your fingers on the table as you recite each word:

Truth, change, justice, beauty.

For you, the kingdom, and the rest of Acazah creation

Your first memory of these words is from a song your mother sang. You were in a bath, and she was watching over you. Nowadays, repeating them makes you feel safe, like you’re back on firm ground after a long voyage.

But alas, now the dandelions are breaching the earth again, the Kingdom is changing faster and faster, and you are reminded that, unlike the Kingdom, you are not eternal.

# Successor

You deliberately have no children of your own, and have avoided growing too close to anyone else's. Some say this is wise because such bonds could wear on your commitment to impartiality, a central facet of Justice — a saying surely true for the unwise.

Fortunately, ten years ago, you anticipated the problem this would cause, and tasked your most trusted advisor with identifying five candidate heirs. You told her to pick out children, some of whom should be chosen based on their virtues, some based on their skills, and some taken from a random page on the Kingdom’s census.

Your advisor worked at the task with diligence, and spent much time away, which gave you room to think.

And you asked her to tell you nothing of the candidates, until today.

Now, sitting in your chamber, you ask:

“Where are the candidates?”

And she answers:

“Your Majesty — They arrive here — at noon.”

You nod.

# Lyon

Your advisor opens the main chamber doors and you see two figures, the smaller of which begins running towards you. It is a young blonde boy.

“I am Lyon!”

He yells, then starts talking about how he wants to be a knight....

items.title: GPT-6 Astra Covertly Underperforms on Safety Research Tasks
items.content:
For a while, UK AISI, Redwood Research and others have been concerned specifically with the possibility that AIs would sabotage safety research, and have invested in looking for signs that this may be happening. This was also a key element in AI 2027, and in many threat models of how the future goes badly.

It is easy to understand why this form of misalignment could be uniquely dangerous. Differentially sabotaging safety research could preserve and expand misalignment through model generations in escalating fashion, with fatal consequences. A misaligned AI could ensure a misaligned successor.

It is also easy to understand why this is an extremely alarming thing to discover, even if the particular example or model involved is not directly dangerous. Silently and differentially sabotaging safety research is perhaps the most fundamentally misaligned thing a model could do.

This also seemed like a rather silly and paranoid thing to be checking. Why would AIs be sabotaging safety work? Even if the AI was misaligned, one would say, surely it would not be so misaligned as to wish future AIs were misaligned and unsafe in general, in non-specific fashion and engage in silent sabotage, and there is no other reason to do this, so this will never come up.

Even if they did sabotage things, surely they would not hide this action from their Chain of Thought (CoT) and it would be obvious.

This certainly wouldn’t be a practical problem that actively hurt real safety work.

Well, we have some bad news, echoing some past similar anecdotal warnings.

items.title: Estimating Our Tail Fire Risk
items.content:
In many
disasters
sheltering in place can make a

lot
of sense, but what about fire?  As someone who lives in one of the
densest municipalities in the country, with 3-story wooden buildings
packed close together, is fire likely enough to rule out any kind of
"stay put" approach?  After having Claude do some rough calculations I
think probably not.

Very few houses are lost to fire anymore, but this is mostly
downstream from putting a lot of effort into suppression.  From when a
fire is reported until firefighters are on the scene is typically an
impressive three
minutes, and they can very quickly be delvering massive amounts of
water onto a fire anywhere in the city.  If an emergency were bad
enough to break or overwhelm this system, a fire anywhere could lead
to city-wide distruction.

Still, I really didn't have a good sense of scale here. If we had a
month-long fire suppression outage, are we talking 10%, 1%, 0.1% chance of fire?
Historically, I would have tried to do a BOTEC,
but these days I set Claude on the problem.  I started with Opus 5.5,
but after it didn't seem to be doing a great job I spent $29.93 to put
Fable 5.1 on the problem (prompts).
I don't know if Claude would beat an expert here, but after skimming
what it did I think it's well above my historical level of modeling.

It estimated from historical fires, and thought our monthly risk was
~1% (but could easily be 5x higher or lower), and if our block worked
together in a disaster we might reduce risk by 4x.  It also thought
that my dad's house in Medford (less dense) was ~4x safer, as was my
sister's house in Brattleboro VT (even less dense).  If you want to
play with it for your house, feel free to point an LLM at the
code.

items.title: Help your friends get ADHD and depression meds
items.content:
For all my efforts at deliberate practicing rationality, by far the most actionable way to self-improve is "get on ADHD or depression meds, if you need them."

Your friends with ADHD and depression struggle to summon the motivation and focus necessary to get themselves a teledoc who can give them such meds. One of the most useful things you can do is sit them down and say "hey, wanna do the steps here to get some meds?" and then stare at them until they do.

(or, until they say "really I do not want that actually.")

This brought to you by ~2 years of Feedbackloop-first Rationality workshops and Thinking Assistance (where it often seemed like the most impactful bits were the 10 minutes of getting someone to sit down and get an appointment with a psychiatrist)

Edit: I realize sometimes ADHD and depression meds are bad for you and/or finding the right ones is nontrivial. But, I think there are many people for whom it's obviously the correct thing to try, it just takes executive function and sustained focus that they are critically lacking.

I think this is much better, if available, than pretty much any other action you can take, because once it's working it requires very little continuous willpower to sustain, and is the biggest single life upgrade I've seen many people take (the only contenders are "switch job" and "break up with partner who is bad for you.")

(I haven't tried CBT, my impression was it was a lot more work)

If you are a friend who is able to help someone make good decisions about what sort of meds might or might not make sense, that's great too. (It is unfortunately maybe more work than "just stare at them until they do it.")
